title: Handwriting is Thinking
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Jamie Lee Clark's DistillED newsletter argues that handwriting's cognitive benefit comes not from tradition but from its enforced slowness. Because handwriting can't keep pace with speech, older students are forced to summarize and rephrase rather than transcribe verbatim, deepening processing; younger children benefit differently, as the physical act of forming letters by hand builds stronger visual/memory circuitry than typing or tracing. Clark cites Jared Cooney Horvath's framing that 'effort shapes memory' and handwriting is itself a form of thinking, along with the James and Engelhardt (2012) study showing hand-printed letters activate reading circuitry more strongly than typed or traced ones. The piece explicitly avoids being anti-technology, instead urging teachers to match the tool to the task and student developmental stage rather than treating typing and handwriting as interchangeable.
points: Reframes handwriting's advantage as a function of its slowness, not sentimental tradition.
Distinguishes benefits for older fluent writers (compression/rephrasing during note-taking) versus young children (letter-formation memory building).
Cites Jared Cooney Horvath's principle that effort shapes memory, summarized as 'handwriting is thinking.'
References James and Engelhardt (2012) showing hand-printed letters activate reading circuitry more than typed/traced letters.
Concludes with a practical 'match the tool to the task' framing rather than a blanket anti-typing stance.
quotes: Handwriting is slower than typing. It can't keep pace with speech or rapid thinking in the way a keyboard can, and that's often treated as a weakness.
Yet the evidence suggests the opposite: handwriting's advantage isn't the pen itself, but the slowness it imposes.
This isn't an argument against technology or in favour of tradition. It's an argument that the pace at which we write changes how we learn.
unable to keep pace with speech, they're forced to compress and rephrase rather than copy word-for-word
forming a letter by hand, which appears to build a different, stronger kind of memory than recognising a letter on a screen or pressing a key
the underlying principle to recognise is that effort shapes memory; handwriting is thinking
letters children learned by printing activated the brain's reading circuitry more strongly than letters learned by typing or tracing, even when the children were just looking at the letters afterward
Match the Tool to the Task — neither handwriting nor typing is universally better.
